svg.title: Three cloud connection models: direct access, gateway hairpin and the hybrid in between
svg.desc: In direct cloud access the branch sends selected application traffic straight to the Internet while other traffic still backhauls to a regional hub. In the gateway model SaaS traffic is tunnelled to the best-performing gateway site and only then routed to the Internet. The hybrid runs both and chooses per application by measured performance. The choice is about determinism and who carries the SLA, not about bandwidth.
svg.text: Three ways to reach the cloud, and the traffic that does not take the new path
The design question is not "how much bandwidth" but "is latency predictable, and who carries the SLA when it is not"
1 · DIRECT CLOUD ACCESS (DIA)
branch
Internet
best path per app
SaaS
all other traffic still backhauls via regional hub / data centre / CNF
path is dropped from the candidate set when unreachable or underperforming
2 · ACCESS THROUGH A GATEWAY (CLIENT SITE → GATEWAY SITE)
client site
no DIA allowed
gateway site
policy + security
SaaS
tunnelled to the best-performing gateway site, then routed to the Internet — hairpin latency is the price of central control
different client sites and applications may use different gateway sites and paths
3 · HYBRID — BOTH, DECIDED PER APPLICATION
branch
DIA
gateway
per-app steering
SaaS
whichever path measures better wins; this is what most enterprises end up running, whether they planned it or not
What actually decides the model
determinism, not bandwidth
Internet: cheap, best-effort, latency varies by hour and by route.
VPN over Internet: encrypted but inherits the same variance — jitter kills chatty traffic.
Dedicated circuit / cloud exchange: predictable latency and loss, contractual SLA, per-Mbps price.
who carries the SLA
On the Internet nobody does: the path crosses several providers with no end-to-end commitment.
On a dedicated circuit the provider commits to latency and loss — insist those numbers appear,
not just "10 Gbps": 10 Gbps at 3% loss can be worse than 1 Gbps at 0.05% for small transactions.
what to write into the design
per application class: which path, what RTT ceiling, what loss ceiling, what happens when it is breached.
per site: is local Internet egress allowed, and if so who inspects that traffic.
per region: where the cloud region physically sits, because the RTT floor is geography, not engineering.
"Plenty of bandwidth" answers a question nobody asked. Determinism answers the one the business asked.
Bandwidth grows with money; determinism grows only with engineering and contracts.
Both paths must exist before you need them — a fallback that has never carried traffic is not a fallback.
DIA is a policy decision as much as a routing one: once branches egress locally, every local device is an Internet-facing edge.
